Who cares about the iPad mini?
All signs point to a new iPad mini arriving today. (Bear in mind, of course, that signs can be wrong.) Which raises an important question: Who cares?
When it was first unveiled in 2012 the mini seemed like the tablet of the future. Attractive, portable, and capable, it had all the ingredients for success. But since then it’s been squeezed by developments at either end of the range. 
iPads have gained bigger screens and more powerful specs at the upper end, and are now suitable for work and entertainment in a way that the diminutive mini can’t match. On the other hand, why buy an iPad mini as well as a phone when you can get a big-screen iPhone such as the 18 Pro Max or Duo and have a capable device that can fulfil both functions? The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, very nearly as big as that of the original mini and not far behind its current 8.3 inches. And the Duo fits that screen into a far more pocketable chassis.
The iPad mini doesn’t even have affordability to recommend it these days, starting at a scarcely budget-friendly $599. The cheap option is the standard iPad at $449, and that comes with a bigger display.
Today’s challenge will be to make the iPad mini relevant again. An OLED screen is a nice idea, but is it enough to shift perceptions of a product that faces superior alternatives in every direction? What about an IP rating and a 2nm processor? My colleague Mahmoud Itani thinks the iPad mini is ready to become the best tablet for everyone, but it won’t be easy.

This week could see Apple add a third entry to that list. Does a touchscreen MacBook make sense? Not really, as we discuss in this week’s Apple Breakfast column, but that doesn’t mean it will fail.

Steve Jobs on touchscreens
When Apple released the iPad in 2010, Steve Jobs described why adding a touchscreen to one of Apple’s existing laptops wasn’t the right move:
“We’ve done tons of user testing on this, and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives a great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off; it doesn’t work. It’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal, hence touchpads for a notebook. That’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.”
How will Apple sell its new touchscreen Mac to the public? According to Mark Gurman, it will be billed as an “optional” feature rather than a primary one, not unlike the Touch Bar. And, well, we all know how that went.

title: Apple Announces OLED MacBook Pro With Touch Display
content:
Apple today announced a new high-end MacBook Pro, which is available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. The new device has a PROLED XDR display that supports touch gestures, and a glowing rear Apple logo.


Pricing on the ‌MacBook Pro‌ starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. 

OLED paired with advanced algorithms in the display engine and factory calibration for "exceptional brightness, striking contrast, and vivid true-to-life colors."

The display offers up to 2000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness, along with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. A display engine controls the color and luminance of each pixel, compensating for content, temperature, environment, and pixel use. ProMotion technology is available with refresh rates ranging from 10Hz to 120Hz. An antireflective coating cuts down on glare in bright lighting conditions, and there is an option to order the new ‌MacBook Pro‌ with a nano-texture display. 


We're glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You've gotta touch it to believe it. https://t.co/BLiGkGaefL
— John Ternus (@johnternus) October 28, 2026




A touch sensor is built directly in the display panel, so there is no added latency. Apple says touch interactions feel "incredibly responsive and refined." Users can scroll through a webpage with a swipe, pinch to zoom in on a photo, drag and drop slides from one presentation to another, and double-tap a window to have it fill the screen.

A new hinge design offers more stability when using touch, and advanced video stabilization smooths the camera feed when using touch on a video call. Apple says macOS automatically translates touch into clicks, so many existing apps will work with touch right away. 

Dynamic Island that takes up less space. The ‌Dynamic Island‌ houses Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. Like on the iPhone, it offers a quick way to see and interact with important information. 

Smaller bezels mean the 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ display is now 16.3 inches in size, while the 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ is now 14.2 inches. 

The new ‌MacBook Pro‌ uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the ‌MacBook Pro‌ models announced back in March, but there is a redesigned thermal architecture that directs warm air away from the display. There is support for up to 128GB of unified memory, and a new six-speaker sound system with 50 percent deeper bass.

MagSafe, and a headphone jack. The new machines support up to four external displays and come with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Fast charging allows the ‌MacBook Pro‌ to be charged to 50 percent in 30 minutes, and up to 16TB storage is available.

title: South Korea Rules Against Apple Over App Store Payment Rules
content:
South Korea has fined Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered it to let developers link to external payment options from their apps, The Associated Press reports.



The Korea Media and Communications Commission found that Apple and Google effectively require developers to use their payment systems, violating a 2021 law intended to allow alternatives. Google was fined 42.9 billion won ($32 million).

Both companies allowed third-party payment services within apps, but charged developers a 26% commission and restricted some features. The regulator said these conditions pushed developers toward Apple and Google's payment systems, while rules against external payment links limited their other options.

The companies must also improve their app review processes. The commission found that some reviews were delayed without clear explanations or information about when they would resume. It separately found that Apple charged South Korean developers higher commissions than overseas developers between 2015 and January 2023.

The Associated Press that it disagrees with the ruling and is considering its legal options. The company says its policies comply with South Korean law and that its payment system helps protect customers against fraud.

title: iOS 27.2 Adds Selfie-Based Age Verification
content:
Apple has added selfie-based age verification in iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2, allowing users in supported regions to demonstrate that they are adults without submitting a credit card or government-issued ID.


The feature estimates whether someone is an adult by analyzing their face, according to a new Apple support document. The capture process involves following onscreen prompts to turn and tilt the head, providing views of the face from four directions.

Apple says the verification process combines processing on the user's device with analysis through Private Cloud Compute. The results are brought together locally, and Apple says the images remain inaccessible to the company and anyone else during processing. After successful verification, the selfie is deleted.

Users who receive an age confirmation prompt may be offered the option, although availability varies by location. Regional requirements determine when adult verification is necessary.

Possible triggers include setting up an Apple Account, installing a software update, accessing apps rated 18+, and adjusting safety controls. Once a user has successfully established their adult status, Apple says further confirmation is unnecessary.

Since the launch of the original iPhone in 2007, Apple has released dozens of versions of iOS, introducing new features, design changes, performance improvements, security updates and more. From the early days of iPhone OS through landmark releases such as iOS 7, iOS 14 and the current iOS 27, each version has changed the way we use the iPhone.
Whether you’re trying to identify the version running on your iPhone, check compatibility before upgrading, or find out which releases are still supported, this guide covers every version of iPhone OS and iOS in chronological order – from the original iPhone OS 1 to iOS 27.
Discover the major features introduced with each release, from the App Store and copy and paste to widgets, Apple Intelligence and the new Siri AI introduced with iOS 27.
Below, you’ll find a complete list of iOS versions in order, along with release dates, key features, compatibility and support information.


What is the latest version of iOS?
The current version of the iPhone operating system is iOS 27, more specifically, iOS 27.2, released on October 26. 
Apple is also continuing to issue security updates for iOS 26 and iOS 18. iOS 26.7.2 and iOS 18.7.11 were also released on October 26.


						

							


iOS version history: Every iOS and the features it brought
There are significant milestones scattered across the iOS timeline:

				
					

				
			Steve Jobs holding the first iPhone at the launch in 2007.
Apple 




iPhone OS (2007): iOS made its debut in 2007 with the first iPhone. However, when Steve Jobs held the little device aloft revealing it to the world for the first time, it wasn’t running iOS 1. Instead, it was reported by Apple to be powered by OS X, the software for the Mac. Over time it was called iPhone OS, until finally gaining its now legendary name in the fourth generation of the software when it was shortened to iOS in 2010.
iPhone OS 2 (2008): The second major release of the iPhone software was groundbreaking because it brought third party apps and introduced the App Store. 
iPhone OS 3 (2009): This update was designed to make it easier to find things, while at the same time adding the ability to have up to 11 pages to the Home Screen. Messages could support MMS, Video recording became possible and it was possible to save voice notes with the Voice Memos app. 
iOS 4 (2010): Apple changed the name to iOS and added the ability to put apps in folders for a better organised Home screen with iOS 4. The FaceTime, iBooks and Game Centre apps also arrived. The iPad also joined the scene, sharing the same operating system as the iPhone.
iOS 5 (2011): iOS 5 was introduced along with the iPhone 4S in 2011, which saw the debut of Siri as a built-in part of the operating system. The Notification Centre was introduced and iCloud arrived bringing synchronization between devices. This was the first time iOS could be installed directly on the iPhone without requiring a computer.
iOS 6 (2012): This is where Apple Maps came onto the scene. Podcasts and Passbook (now Wallet) apps also arrived. iCloud Photo Stream made it easier to share photos with family and friends. iOS 6 was the last with a skeuomorphic design. 
iOS 7 (2013): With iOS 7 iPhone users got a redesigned user interface, which looked a lot more modern with flatter icons. iOS 7 introduced AirDrop and CarPlay.

				
					

				
			iOS 7 had a brand new look (at the time).
Apple




iOS 8 (2014): One of the features of iOS 8 was Continuity, which linked the iPhone, iPad and Mac together, so you could “handoff” tasks from one device to another. Family Sharing also arrived making it easier to manage a child’s iPhone. 
iOS 9 (2015): iOS 9 improved the Notes app, added Apple News, and featured a new Night Shift mode that removed some of the blue light that can disturb circadian rhythms and stop someone sleeping. 
iOS 10 (2016): There were updates to Messages and changes to the Photos app in iOS 10. A new Home app brought HomeKit control. Maps got a redesign. Universal Clipboard meant that users could copy something on a Mac and paste it on an iPhone, for example. 
iOS 11 (2017): Things changed significantly in iOS 11 in 2017 as it brought the first touch and gesture interface, allowing the first iPhone without a Home button – the iPhone X. There was a new Files app making it easier to access content synced or saved in iCloud and the Control Centre got a redesign. 
iOS 12 (2018): Screen Time, Memoji, Group FaceTime and Siri Shortcuts were new in iOS 12. 
iOS 13 (2019): Another major shift came with iOS 13 in 2019, as Apple’s mobile operating system for the iPad split with the iPhone, with iPadOS powering new iPads. Updates to iOS included Dark Mode, new privacy features and the ability to Sign in with Apple and hide your email address. The Photos and Apple Maps apps got a redesign and a swipe-to-type keyboard was added.  
iOS 14 (2020): One of the most notable additions was Back Tap, a feature that effectively turned the back of the iPhone into an extra button. Home Screen widgets and the App Library were also major new features. Starting with iOS 14.2, music recognition was built directly into the operating system via a Shazam button.

				
					

				
			iOS 15 on iPhone 12.
Foundry




iOS 15 (2021): Focus Mode arrived in iOS 15 to help users manage the onslaught of notifications, Live Text and Visual Look up made it possible to interact with text within photos (Live Text) and use the camera to identify objects like plants and animals. The Safari browser received a major interface update as did Maps and the Weather app. Read: iOS 15 vs iOS 14.
iOS 16 (2022): One of the most visible changes in iOS 16 was the complete overhaul of the Lock screen, which allowed users to add widgets for the first time to view data at a glance without unlocking their devices. Apple added Rapid Security Responses so that it could deliver important security patches outside of an iOS update. Read: iOS 16 vs iOS 15.
iOS 17 (2023): NameDrop in iOS 17 made it possible to share information by bringing two iPhones together. Stolen Device Protection added a layer of security by requiring biometric authentication (Face ID or Touch ID) before an Apple ID password could be changed. Live Voicemail meant that iPhone users could get a live transcription of a message. Read: iOS 17 vs iOS 16.
iOS 18 (2024): The iOS 18 update laid the groundwork for Apple’s subsequent AI initiatives. There was also a complete redesign of the Photos app, a dedicated Passwords app, and Control Center Customization. Read: iOS 18 vs iOS 17.
iOS 26 (2025): Rather than progress to iOS 19, Apple aligned the numbering of all its operating systems according to the year with iOS 26. It wasn’t just a name change though, there was a significant visual and functional overhaul with a Liquid Glass design language. Big changes also came to the Phone app with Call Screening and Hold Assist. Live Translations make it easy to communicate with foreign friends and colleagues. The Camera app had a simplifying redesign and a Games app that integrated Game Centre features. Here’s how iOS 26 and iOS 18 compare.
iOS 27 (2026): iOS 27 launched in September 2026, including a massive overhaul of Siri, better Apple Intelligence integration, improved photo and camera tools, and parental control enhancements. Here’s how iOS 26 and iOS 27 compare.

				
					

				
			
Foundry



							




List of iOS versions and latest versions
Here’s a breakdown of all the versions of iOS that have been released, when they were released, when they were last updated, and the latest iOS version.

Which iOS versions are supported by Apple?
iOS 27 is Apple’s current iPhone operating system and the version receiving new features and functionality. It can run on the iPhone 11 and newer, as well as the iPhone SE (2nd generation) and later.
Every iPhone that supports iOS 26 also supports iOS 27, but Apple is continuing to maintain iOS 26 with security updates, at least for now. On October 26, Apple released iOS 26.7.2 and iOS 18.7.11 alongside iOS 27.2, allowing users who haven’t yet upgraded to iOS 27 to continue receiving important security fixes.
Apple also periodically releases security updates for considerably older versions of iOS on devices that can no longer upgrade to a newer release.


						

							


Which iOS versions get security updates only?
Even after Apple stops developing new features for older versions of iOS, it can continue to issue security updates for devices that cannot run the latest operating system. As explained in How long does Apple support iPhones?, this means some older iPhones can continue receiving security fixes years after they stop getting major iOS upgrades.
In August 2026, for example, Apple released iOS 18.7.10 with security fixes for the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max and iPhone XR. Those are the iPhones that remain on iOS 18 because they cannot upgrade to iOS 26 or iOS 27. Apple’s newer iPhones are generally expected to move to a newer version of iOS to receive the latest security fixes.
There was no equivalent iOS 18 update on September 28, when Apple released iOS 27.0.1 and iOS 26.7.1. The latter patched a CoreGraphics vulnerability that Apple says may have been exploited in highly targeted attacks against versions of iOS earlier than iOS 27. iOS 26.7.1 is available for the iPhone 11 and later.
Support extends even further back. On May 11, 2026, Apple released iOS 15.8.8 for the iPhone 6s, iPhone 7 and first-generation iPhone SE, and iOS 16.7.16 for the iPhone 8, iPhone 8 Plus and iPhone X. Both updates included security fixes. This doesn’t mean that Apple will continue to support these iOS versions. 
That means the following older iPhones were still receiving some form of software support in 2026:
iPhone 6s and 6s Plus
iPhone SE (1st generation)
iPhone 7 and 7 Plus
iPhone 8 and 8 Plus
iPhone X
iPhone XR
iPhone XS and XS Max
Many of those iPhones appear in Apple’s list of Obsolete and Vintage iPhones, demonstrating that software security support can continue even after normal hardware servicing has become restricted or ended. 
The oldest of these is the iPhone 6s from 2015, meaning Apple was still issuing software fixes for it more than ten years after launch.
It is not yet clear whether Apple will release further iOS 15 and iOS 16 security updates now that iOS 27 has launched. Neither received an update alongside iOS 27 on September 14 or the September 28 security releases, but Apple has not announced that support has formally ended.
Apple has occasionally supported even older software when necessary to keep essential services working. In January 2026, for example, it released an update for iOS 12 to extend certificates used by features including iMessage, FaceTime and device activation beyond January 2027. That meant even devices as old as the iPhone 5s received an update in 2026.


						

							


Which iPhones support which iOS versions?
Luckily, many iPhones are able to run supported versions of iOS. We run through which iPhone supports which version of iOS in a separate article: iOS compatibility: Find out the latest version your iPhone can run. You may also find this at a glance chart useful:

				
					

				
			
The version of iOS each iPhone can run.

Foundry







						

							




So, there it is. A potted history of iOS. Want to know about all the versions of macOS? Read: Mac OS X and macOS: Every version released so far. You can also find out what the latest version of macOS is.

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro: OLED, design and release date rumors
content:
Macworld





Apple could unveil its first touchscreen MacBook Pro today, October 28, 2026, alongside its “Pro and Tell” media experience in Los Angeles. Reports point to OLED displays, a lighter chassis, a redesigned hinge and a possible Dynamic Island camera cutout. Apple has not yet confirmed the touchscreen models or their specifications.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way.
The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrated its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.
Apple separately announced the standard 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro on October 27. It retains the existing design and non-touchscreen display, with preorders beginning October 28 and availability from November 6. See our M6 MacBook Pro guide for that model.
There are still questions over pricing and availability. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures could make the touchscreen models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro, while touch support is expected to remain exclusive to Apple’s premium laptops initially. Read on for everything we know about the touchscreen MacBook Pro’s expected release date, design, specifications and price, including what Apple could announce on October 28.


Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
Apple media experience confirmed for October 28; touchscreen MacBook Pro announcement expected
On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026. This is expected to be the introduction of new Macs, including the touchscreen MacBook Pro.


Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026





Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman’s latest reporting points to an October 28 announcement for the touchscreen MacBook Pro, following the standard M6 model’s announcement on October 27. 
Earlier reports offered a broader launch window and raised the possibility of delays. Speaking in a Power On podcast on October 1, Gurman said he expected the touchscreen MacBook announcement as early as October, potentially slipping to November. The laptops are reportedly being tested with macOS 27.2.
In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction. In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8.6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.
Gurman’s more recent reporting points to an October announcement and November availability. However, the launch was previously predicted for early 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into early 2027. He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule. 


						

							


Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen? 
Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips
Both Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo have reported that Apple is developing MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreen displays as part of a major redesign. The feature is expected to debut on the high-end MacBook Pro models powered by Apple’s Pro and Max chips, making them the first Macs to support direct touch input.
Apple is expected to use the touchscreen as a key differentiator for its professional laptops, further separating the MacBook Pro from the more affordable MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.
There is also speculation that Apple could rebrand the flagship model as the MacBook Ultra. According to one report from a source said to be familiar with Apple’s plans, the company intends to expand its “Ultra” branding beyond the Mac Studio and Apple silicon chips. However, this claim has not been corroborated by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman or analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, so it should be treated with caution.
For now, the technology appears set to remain exclusive to the MacBook Pro lineup. Neither the MacBook Air nor the MacBook Neo is expected to gain touchscreen support in the near term. However, Kuo believes Apple could eventually expand the technology to other MacBook models if the touchscreen MacBook Pro proves successful.
The MacBook Air may be the next candidate for a touchscreen upgrade, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely before 2028 or 2029. Some reports also indicate that the Air could adopt OLED display technology before then, albeit without touch functionality.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro Design
Lighter design expected
Punch hole for the FaceTime camera

				
					

				
			The last time Apple included touch with the MacBook was the TouchBar, which was a flop. But this time could it work out better for Apple? 
Foundry




Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to have a substantially lighter design than current models, but it may not be significantly thinner. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has revised his earlier expectations for a slimmer body while maintaining that Apple has redesigned and consolidated internal components to reduce weight. 
Gurman also reports a redesigned cooling system intended to improve airflow through the hinge while reducing weight.
One of the most significant visual changes could be the removal of the display notch. Reports from display analysts and Bloomberg suggest Apple may replace the current notch with a hole-punch camera cutout, allowing for more usable screen space around the sensor. In early 2026, Gurman went a step further, claiming the new MacBook Pro could adopt an iPhone-like Dynamic Island interface built around the camera cutout.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is also expected to retain its traditional laptop design, complete with a full keyboard and large trackpad, rather than becoming a hybrid tablet device.
Other rumoured design changes include:
A lighter chassis, although the latest reporting suggests it may not be thinner.
OLED display technology.
A hole-punch FaceTime camera replacing the notch.
Possible Dynamic Island-style functionality.
A reinforced hinge designed to minimise screen movement when the display is touched.
These changes would help distinguish the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the entry-level MacBook Neo while giving Apple’s flagship laptop its most substantial design update in years.


						

							


Which chip will feature in the touchscreen MacBook?
M5 Pro and M5 Max
Early rumors suggested that Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro would feature M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but more recent reports indicate that Apple has changed its plans. The redesigned OLED models are now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, with Apple potentially skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation entirely.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman in June 2026, Apple has revised its chip roadmap to accelerate development of the AI-focused M7 generation. The change could bring the M7 chips to market around six months earlier, with significantly improved on-device AI capabilities. The ongoing DRAM and NAND shortages may also have influenced Apple’s decision, although they are not thought to be the primary reason. Apple has already increased Mac and iPad prices in response to rising memory costs. Read more about Apple’s reported chip roadmap changes.
Separately, Apple has launched the 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip.
There has also been speculation that Apple could introduce its own 5G modem to a future MacBook Pro, enabling cellular connectivity without Wi-Fi or an iPhone hotspot. However, there is little concrete evidence that cellular connectivity will be part of the touchscreen redesign.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Display
Tandem OLED display
Touchscreen interface
The display is expected to be the headline upgrade of Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro. Multiple reports suggest Apple will replace the current Liquid Retina XDR (mini-LED) panel with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing MacBook Pro technology closer to the Ultra Retina XDR display used in the latest iPad Pro.
According to analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, Apple is planning to introduce OLED touch panels in the MacBook Pro in late 2026 or early 2027. The new display is expected to be thinner, more power-efficient, and capable of delivering deeper blacks, higher contrast, richer colours, and improved HDR performance than today’s mini-LED screens.
Reports indicate that both the 14-inch and 16-inch models will use advanced tandem OLED technology, which combines two OLED layers to achieve higher brightness levels while maintaining excellent energy efficiency. Apple first introduced this technology with the M4 iPad Pro and is expected to bring a similar implementation to the MacBook Pro.
The touchscreen functionality will reportedly rely on on-cell touch technology, which integrates touch sensors directly into the display rather than adding a separate layer. This approach helps keep the panel thin while supporting multi-touch input.
If the rumours prove accurate, the move to a tandem OLED touchscreen would represent the biggest display upgrade in the MacBook Pro’s history and one of the most significant changes to the lineup in years.

				
					

				
			The iPad Pro has a tandem OLED display, the type of display that could make its way into the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Brady Snyder / Foundry



							


Touchscreen MacBook Interface 

				
					

				
			macOS 27 could have some hidden touchscreen features. 

Foundry




Apple is not expected to turn macOS into iPadOS, but reports suggest macOS 27 could include subtle design changes to make the Mac easier to use with touch input.
Rather than replacing the traditional desktop experience, Apple is reportedly working on a touch-tuned interface that adapts depending on how the device is being used. When touch input is detected, interface elements such as menus, buttons, and controls may automatically enlarge to make them easier to tap. When using a mouse or trackpad, macOS would revert to its familiar point-and-click layout.
Gurman’s latest report also describes dial-like menus appearing around the user’s finger. Touch is expected to provide an additional input method alongside the keyboard and trackpad, rather than replacing them.
The touchscreen itself is expected to support standard gestures such as tapping, scrolling, and zooming, while still allowing users to switch between touch, trackpad, and mouse input.
Further clues appeared in the macOS 27.2 beta on October 5. MacRumors reported new code references to touch gestures in Safari, Photos, Notes and Quick Look. These could support a future touchscreen MacBook, but they could also relate to Sidecar, which allows an iPad to act as a Mac display. 
More specific clues appeared in footage shared by itspdfu on October 14. The footage reportedly shows touch-oriented behavior in Safari in macOS 27.2 betas 3 and 4: tabs lift and enlarge while being rearranged, then return to their normal size when dropped into place. Pressing and holding a tab opens a contextual menu that omits the Ask Siri option available with a mouse or trackpad. These changes suggest Apple is preparing Safari for touch input.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Connectivity 
5G connectivity could finally come to the Mac

				
					

				
			The C1X is now available, but the C2 modem could arrive with the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Apple




Beyond the touchscreen display and redesigned chassis, one of the most intriguing rumours surrounding the next-generation MacBook Pro is built-in cellular connectivity.
Apple has spent the past several years developing its own modem technology, beginning with the C-series modem family. Reports suggest the company has explored bringing 5G connectivity to the MacBook lineup, allowing users to connect directly to mobile networks without relying on Wi-Fi or a smartphone hotspot.
In August 2025, Macworld reported that internal Apple code referenced a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip and Apple’s C1 modem. This suggests Apple has experimented with cellular-equipped MacBooks, althogugh it does not establish that the upcoming touchscreen models will offer 5G.
The redesigned MacBook Pro could also benefit from Apple’s growing portfolio of wireless chips. The company’s N-series networking processors, which handle Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Thread connectivity, may eventually replace third-party components throughout the Mac lineup. An updated version of the chip could debut alongside the touchscreen MacBook Pro, improving power efficiency and tighter integration with Apple’s ecosystem.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Price expectations
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple has discussed a $2,899 starting price for the 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro with M5 Pro – a $400 premium over the current non-touchscreen M5 Pro model. 
Apple is also reportedly planning to retain the existing non-touchscreen models alongside the premium touchscreen versions.
Here are the prices for the current standard configurations of the MacBook Pro, which saw prices increase between $300 and $500 in June 2026.
14-inch MacBook Pro (non-touchscreen)
$1,999/£1,999: M6 with a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB unified memory, 1TB SSD and Thunderbolt 4.
$2,499/£2,499: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,099/£4,099: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
16-inch MacBook Pro (non-touchscreen)
$2,999/£2,999: M5 Pro with a 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,399/£4,399: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5

title: The touchscreen MacBook Pro completes the circle started 10 years ago
content:
Macworld





October 27, 2016 was a day that shook the laptop market. Some of us are still recovering from what Apple did on that day, and how it lead to insanity amongst devoted Mac users. On that day, Apple introduced the first MacBook Pro with the Touch Bar. And the world was never the same.
Okay, sarcasm aside, the Touch Bar, on the surface, seemed like a good idea at the time. That idea was to provide more dynamic input capabilities than the standard F keys across the top of the keyboard. In our early hands-on of the Touch Bar when it was revealed, Macworld editor Susie Ochs felt like it had potential, despite some lag.
However, the Touch Bar suffered from what seemed like neglect from Apple. Its performance never really improved, and it never evolved beyond those early days. Five years ago, I wrote about how I really tried to like the Touch Bar, but I was ready to move on. I could never adjust my workflow to the accommodate the strip screen, and prefer having physical function keys that I can press without hunting them down with my eyes first.
And now, 10 years after the Touch Bar introduction and almost exactly three years since its discontinuation, Apple will reportedly release a touchscreen MacBook Pro. The Touch Bar was seen by some as an Apple compromise for not having a touchscreen–there was even speculation that the Touch Bar was a precursor to a touchscreen Mac, but Apple shot down that theory. Now, as Apple prepares to launch what most people had given up on, the excitement of those early Touch Bar days can be felt once again. 
But I can’t help but wonder if the touchscreen MacBook Pro will follow the same pattern as the Touch Bar: Impressive at first, but as time goes on, it doesn’t seem necessary. According to rumors, Apple will treat touch as an option rather than a necessity, despite attaching a hefty premium to touchscreen devices. macOS Golden Gate is said to be retooled to work with fingers, but Apple will need to be active in touchscreen development to make it more successful than the Touch Bar. 
But for now, let’s enjoy the anticipation and promise that Apple’s first touchscreen Mac brings. And pour one out for the Touch Bar that had to die so the touchscreen MacBook could live.
creator: Macworld

title: MacPaw Launches 'Eney' AI Assistant for Mac and iPhone
content:
MacPaw has launched Eney, a proactive AI assistant for Mac and iPhone that the company says understands what is happening across a user's apps, files, and system, prepares the next step, and asks before it acts.


On Mac, Eney offers copy-triggered suggestions, bot-free meeting transcription with notes and follow-ups, and ready-made workflows such as Morning Brief and Plan My Day. An "Eney Wand" (Option-W) acts on whatever is dragged over to it, and can translate text, convert prices, turn dates into calendar events, and extract text from images. 

The app also surfaces Mac care warnings for low disk space, memory pressure, and crashing apps, and connects to Apple Mail, Calendar, and Reminders out of the box, plus Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Slack, Notion, Jira, and Linear. 

MacPaw calls Eney "proactive, never autonomous", since by default it asks before sending a message, changing an event, or moving a file. Eney is also the first product powered by MacPaw's own AI stack, including a memory layer called Mnemos that MacPaw says manages only Eney's own memory and never reads or changes user files.


Eney for Mac is available to download from eney.ai and requires an Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15 or later. There's a free 14-day trial that includes 10,000 AI credits, after which an AI credits subscription is required. A Starter plan with 10,000 AI credits costs $14.99/month, a Boost plan with 25,000 credits costs $29.99/month, and a Power plan with 50,000 credits costs $49.99/month.

title: What to do about a lost or stolen iPhone before it becomes a bigger mess
content:
Marking a stolen iPhone as lost instantly locks your data, but the real race is securing your accounts before the thief does. Here is how to lock it down and recover.

What do I do if my iPhone was stolen?
Your first instinct may be to retrace the day and check under car seats, behind couch cushions, or anywhere you recently used your iPhone. Do that, but secure the missing iPhone immediately while you search so a simple loss doesn't turn into stolen access to your accounts.
The hardware is replaceable. What's harder to replace is the access your iPhone carries, including passwords, payment cards, verification codes, and often the only trusted connection to your Apple Account.
A locked iPhone is difficult to break into when nobody else knows the passcode. The danger rises sharply if a thief has watched you enter it, because that code can expose saved passwords, account recovery options, and other security settings.

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro to Debut Today With These 5 Features
content:
Some reports have suggested the new high-end MacBook Pro models that Apple is expected to announce today might not be called ‌MacBook Pro‌s at all. They could in fact be something altogether new and more exciting – "MacBook Ultra," perhaps – marketed as the company's top-tier laptop offering. The machines are expected to sit above the current M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, rather than replace them, suggesting the latter will remain in Apple's lineup.


One thing to state up front is that Apple is expected to stick with the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for its touchscreen MacBook models. Apple reportedly plans to skip what would have been the "M6 Pro" and "M6 Max" for more powerful "M7 Pro" and "M7 Max" chips. Apple announced the new entry-level 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ with the M6 chip yesterday, ahead of pre-orders opening today, but the first "MacBook Ultra" models will use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, after which second-generation models will come with M7 Pro and Max chips in late 2027.

MacRumors' sources earlier indicated: the OLED iPad mini arrived on Monday, and the M6 iMac and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro followed yesterday. The new touchscreen models are expected to debut today at Apple's "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles and become available for pre-order at 10:10 a.m. Pacific Time, with Bloomberg reporting that availability could begin as early as November 6. Recent reports have referred to the machines simply as new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models, so the final name remains uncertain.

Below, we've listed the features and changes we are expecting for the new high-end MacBook Pro models.

OLED Display

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo say Apple is readying OLED technology for these models, and industry reports corroborate their claims. Samsung Display is said to be making the panels exclusively, and the supplier has invested heavily in an 8.6-generation OLED production line in South Korea. The line reached a key milestone for mass production in May.

OLED presents an overall upgrade over the current mini-LED display technology, bringing deeper colors and a higher contrast ratio with true blacks. In an OLED display, individual pixels turn off instead of dimming when not activated, so there's less light leakage and better power efficiency. OLED displays also tend to have better HDR output than mini-LED, but they don't always match mini-LED brightness levels.

Touchscreen

The new ‌MacBook Pro‌ is expected to become the first Mac to support touch input directly on the display. It's a notable shift from Apple's longstanding position against bringing touchscreen functionality to the Mac. 

Apple previously experimented with touch controls through the OLED Touch Bar on earlier ‌MacBook Pro‌ models, but the feature was ultimately discontinued following a lukewarm reception. Rather than positioning the ‌MacBook Pro‌ as a touch-centric device like the ‌iPad‌, Apple is reportedly planning to let users move seamlessly between touch and traditional trackpad or mouse input across the system.

There are features in ‌macOS Golden Gate‌ that hint at a future touchscreen Mac. Apple added direct touch input to Sidecar so users can tap and interact with macOS elements when using the ‌iPad‌ as a Mac display. macOS Golden Gate‌ also supports an iPhone-style pull-to-refresh option, and it can be used across apps like Safari, Mail, News, Podcasts, and Calendar. A pull-to-refresh option makes the most sense on a touch display.

Reinforced Hinge

Apple has reportedly developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched. Apple is apparently aware of the same issue that plagues existing touch PCs.

Lighter Design

Gurman has reported that Apple is working to make the OLED MacBook Pro thinner, as part of the company's plan to create "the thinnest and lightest products in their categories across the whole tech industry." (Think the latest iPad Pro and iPad Air – two of the thinnest devices the company has ever made.) Indeed, the reporter said there's a good chance that the next MacBook Pro model will represent a "true overhaul" for the laptop, thanks to the combination of the OLED display and thinner design.

reported that the OLED MacBook Pro models would have "thinner and lighter" frames. Then again in November 2025, he said the touchscreen models would have "a thinner chassis."

However, Gurman has walked back somewhat on his previous reporting that Apple's upcoming touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro will be thinner than current models. "I don't think it'll be significantly thinner in the end," he said in early October 2026.

reports that Apple has also reworked the cooling system to improve airflow through the hinge while helping to reduce the laptop's weight.

Dynamic Island

The MacBook Ultra could ditch the current notch used in the MacBook Pro models for a display cutout potentially similar to the iPhone's Dynamic Island, according to Bloomberg. Such a move would mirror Apple's iPhone evolution, since the iPhone's notch became the current Dynamic Island starting with the iPhone 14 Pro models in 2022. 

As with the iPhone‌, the Mac ‌Dynamic Island‌ will be interactive and it will contextually expand based on the app or Mac feature in use. The change should address long-standing user complaints about the notch, which physically ingresses into the macOS menu bar.

Price Changes

There is no doubt that Apple will unveil the new MacBook Pro models as ultra-premium products carrying price tags that are higher than the current MacBook Pro 14-inch and 16-inch models. Apple increased the prices of all its Macs in June 2026 – MacBook Pro‌ pricing went up $300 – so the "MacBook Ultra" will likely be even more expensive than expected. ‌

Bloomberg reported this week that Apple has discussed charging $2,899 for the new 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip, which would mean a starting price of at least $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Hold onto your wallets!

title: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4: Complete guide to price, specs and features
content:
Macworld





In September 2026 Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, with both models focusing much more heavily on health monitoring, Apple Intelligence and battery efficiency than on physical redesigns. Series 12 remains Apple’s mainstream premium smartwatch, while Ultra 4 continues as the larger, tougher model aimed at endurance sports, outdoor activities and diving. Both Apple Watches went on sale on September 18.
The biggest upgrade shared by both watches is Apple’s all-new Health Sensing System, which combines redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors with larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Apple says it provides the most accurate heart-rate sensing of any wearable it tested. Background heart-rate readings are now taken every five seconds, while HRV can be measured as often as every five minutes – 60 times and 24 times more frequently respectively than on Series 11.
That additional data powers another major addition: Readiness, which gives users a 0–10 score based on recent activity, sleep, vitals and recovery data, and updates during the day. Both watches also use Apple’s new S11 chip, which enables Siri AI and a collection of Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, faster Shazam, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are not available yet. Apple says both will arrive as beta features later in 2026, initially in English.
The most dramatic hardware improvement is reserved for the Ultra 4: Apple has increased its normal-use battery-life rating from 42 hours to 50 hours, Low Power Mode from 72 to 84 hours, and introduced workout modes capable of tracking for up to 45 hours. Series 12 remains rated at 24 hours, although our testing found inconsistent battery life and charging performance, while the aluminium Series 12 gains tougher Ceramic Shield 2 and Apple has brought back a premium ceramic Apple Watch for the first time in years.
The five biggest Apple Watch upgrades for 2026
New Health Sensing System with substantially more frequent heart-rate and HRV monitoring.
Readiness score for daily recovery and training guidance. 
S11 chip, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence, including Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which are both coming in a later software update.
Much longer Ultra 4 battery life, rising from 42 to 50 hours, with up to 45 hours of extended workout tracking.
New materials and durability, including Ceramic Shield 2 on aluminium Series 12 and the return of ceramic Series 12 models.
The rumours were broadly right that this wouldn’t be a major redesign, and also correctly predicted the emphasis on health, Siri AI and ceramic materials. However, rumours of Touch ID have not materialised, there is still no blood-glucose sensor, and the Series 12 hasn’t gained longer quoted battery life despite speculation about a larger battery. Starting prices are unchanged, although the 46mm Series 12 costs more.

				
					

				
			
Your watch knows how you are feeling. Do you? 

Apple




Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4: Specs compared


FeatureApple Watch Series 12Apple Watch Ultra 4

Health Sensing SystemNew optical/electrical sensorsSame new system

BatteryUp to 24 hours; 38 hours Low PowerUp to 50 hours; 84 hours Low Power

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 release date and availability
Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 on September 9, 2026. Both models went on sale on September 18 and are available from Apple, authorized retailers and participating carriers.
watchOS 27 was released on September 14 for compatible existing Apple Watches.
Both watches are available now, including in the U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and more than 50 other countries and regions.
You can buy them directly from Apple through Apple.com, the Apple Store app and Apple retail stores. They are also available through Apple-authorised retailers and, in the case of cellular models, participating mobile networks.
$389.99 at  Walmart										 | 
																$399 at  Amazon										 | 
																$399 at  Apple United States						
					
$774 at  Amazon										 | 
																$774 at  Walmart										 | 
																$799 at  Apple United States						
					
Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.S. 
Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.K. 


							


Apple Watch Series 12 design

				
					

				
			
The Apple Watch Series 12 in bronze.

David Price / Foundry




The Series 12 does not represent a major external redesign, as the pre-launch rumours suggested. It retains Apple’s familiar rounded-square design and comes in 42mm and 46mm sizes.
Interestingly, the aluminium and titanium cases are fractionally wider than Series 11. The 46mm model measures 46 x 40 x 9.7mm, compared with 46 x 39 x 9.7mm for Series 11. The 42mm version measures 42 x 37 x 9.7mm, compared with 42 x 36 x 9.7mm previously. The screen resolutions remain 416×496 pixels and 374×446 pixels respectively.
Apple continues to offer aluminium and titanium models, but ceramic has returned as a premium case option. Ceramic models are fractionally larger and thicker, measuring 43mm or 47mm tall and 9.85mm thick.
The finishes are:
Aluminium: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black and Space Grey
Titanium: Radiant Gold and Natural
Ceramic: Pearl White and Night Blue
The ceramic options confirm one of the more interesting pre-launch rumours, although Apple opted for Night Blue rather than the dark grey that had also been indicated.
The Series 12 display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina OLED with up to 2,000 nits brightness. Aluminium models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the Ion-X glass used on Series 11. Titanium and ceramic versions use sapphire crystal.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 4 design

				
					

				
			
The rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Apple




The Ultra 4 changes even less externally. It remains a 49mm Grade 5 titanium watch, measuring exactly 49 x 44 x 12mm, with the same 422×514-pixel display and 1,245 sq mm display area as Ultra 3.
It comes in the familiar Natural Titanium and Black Titanium finishes and retains its flat sapphire crystal display, raised protective case edges, prominent Digital Crown and orange-accented Action button.
The Ultra 4 is slightly heavier, however: 63.0g in Natural and 63.1g in Black, compared with 61.6g and 61.8g respectively for Ultra 3.
The display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina display capable of 3,000 nits, so there is no headline screen-brightness upgrade.
Apple hasn’t introduced the rumoured Touch ID fingerprint sensor on the 2026 Apple Watch models. 


						

							


What about the buttons and controls?

				
					

				
			
The side button.

Apple




The physical control layout is essentially unchanged.
Series 12 has:
Digital Crown with haptic feedback
Side button
Strap-release buttons
Ultra 4 adds the familiar:
Customisable Action button
Larger protected Digital Crown
Side button
The Action button can start workouts, mark segments, move to the next interval, activate the torch and perform other user-selected actions.
There is, however, a new single-tap finger-and-thumb gesture in addition to Double Tap and Wrist Flick, providing another way to interact without touching the display.


						

							


Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 health features
The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 share the same new Health Sensing System and Readiness features. Paying more for the Ultra doesn’t get you more advanced core health sensors.

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




More frequent heart-rate and HRV tracking
Both watches have redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors, including larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Background heart-rate readings are taken every five seconds, while heart rate variability (HRV) can be measured as often as every five minutes. These more frequent measurements provide a fuller picture of your activity and recovery throughout the day.
HRV measures variation in the time between heartbeats. The watches distinguish between Recovery HRV, which helps assess shorter-term stress and recovery, and overall HRV, which provides insight into longer-term health trends. Recovery HRV is also included in overnight Vitals, where it is compared with your personal baseline. A new daytime Vitals view shows heart rate and HRV, helping you spot changes outside your usual ranges.
Readiness: Should you push harder or take it easy?
Readiness combines recent activity, training load, daytime and overnight vitals, and sleep data into a score from 0 to 10. It provides one of four recommendations:
Recover: 0–1
Pace Yourself: 2–4
Ready: 5–7
Go For It: 8–10
The score updates throughout the day as you exercise, rest or take a nap. Open the Readiness app to see how activity, vitals and sleep are influencing it.
You’ll need to set up Activity, Sleep and overnight Vitals, enter your health details, and wear the watch to bed for at least seven nights before receiving a score. Readiness is a wellness guide: it doesn’t account for every medical condition or medication and shouldn’t be your sole basis for deciding whether it is safe to exercise.
Returning health features
Both watches retain ECG, high and low heart-rate notifications, irregular-rhythm notifications, blood oxygen tracking, sleep stages, sleep score, sleep apnea notifications and temperature-based Cycle Tracking. These features are also available on earlier compatible Apple Watches, although availability varies by model and region.
Hypertension notifications look for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure over 30-day periods; they don’t provide a blood-pressure reading. The feature also supports earlier compatible models, and availability on Series 12 and Ultra 4 remains subject to regulatory clearance in some regions.
Do the new sensors affect battery life?
In Macwelt’s comparison of the Series 12 and Series 11, Halyna Kubiv recorded more background activity on the newer watch but lower energy consumption during the period after a hike.
That comparison covered a single day, and the watches differed in iPhone pairing and display use. It suggests the additional monitoring can be efficient, but doesn’t prove it has no effect on battery life.


						

							


Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 processor: What processor do they use?
Both watches use Apple’s new S11 chip, replacing the S10 used by Series 11 and Ultra 3.
Apple’s specifications list:
64-bit dual-core processor
4-core Neural Engine
64GB storage
Secure hardware for Audio Intelligence processing
The S10 also had a 64-bit dual-core CPU, four-core Neural Engine and 64GB of storage, so the headline specifications alone don’t reveal how much faster S11 actually is. Apple calls it its “most powerful wearable chip”, but notably hasn’t provided a percentage CPU or GPU performance improvement over S10, and its technical specifications don’t list a separate GPU core count.
That means the more important S11 improvements appear to be what the chip enables rather than raw benchmark performance.
It works with the new Health Sensing System, supports Siri AI and powers the new Audio Intelligence functionality. Apple has also emphasised efficiency, particularly in relation to higher-frequency sensor readings and Ultra 4’s improved battery life.
The new Audio Intelligence system includes a Secure Exclave, a hardware-isolated area of the S11 that processes audio separately and deletes raw audio immediately after processing.


						

							


2026 Apple Watch connectivity

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Connectivity changes are modest. Cellular Series 12 and Ultra 4 models support 5G RedCap and LTE, as did their predecessors, with no newly branded Apple-designed modem.
Both watches also support Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) on 2.4GHz and 5GHz, Bluetooth 5.3, and Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip. Wi-Fi 4 may sound dated, but Apple Watch relies mainly on Bluetooth and has relatively low data requirements.
Satellite connectivity
Satellite communications remain a major distinction between the Series and Ultra families.
Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t have built-in satellite connectivity.
Ultra 4 does, supporting Emergency SOS via satellite and Find My location sharing via satellite when cellular and Wi-Fi aren’t available. 
This is in addition to Messages via Satellite, which arrived in September 2025 with the Apple Watch Ultra 3. That feature lets you send and receive personal messages when your watch has no cellular or Wi-Fi coverage. However, Messages via satellite is available only in the US, Canada, Mexico and Japan. The new Emergency SOS via satellite is available in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Australia, New Zealand, various European countries, Japan and Mexico. No cellular plan is required for Emergency SOS via satellite.
This is broadly what had been expected before launch: Satellite remains primarily an Ultra feature rather than migrating to the regular Series watch.


						

							


2026 Apple Watch battery and charging: What’s new?

				
					

				
			
Charging the Apple Watch. 

Apple




Apple Watch Series 12
Apple rates Series 12 for:
Up to 24 hours normal use
Up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode
Up to 10 hours of outdoor workout tracking
Those first two figures are unchanged from Series 11, so despite rumours that Apple was working on a larger battery, there is no increase in Apple’s quoted everyday battery life.
Apple claims improved endurance from a short charge.
Apple quotes the following charging figures for Series 12:
80 percent in around 30 minutes
Up to 12 hours of use from a 15-minute charge
Up to 10 hours of sleep tracking from five minutes of charging
Apple also rated Series 11 for an 80 percent charge in around 30 minutes, and up to eight hours of normal use from a 15-minute charge.
In our Apple Watch Series 12 review, we recorded 51 and 40 hours of battery life across two runs – an average of 45.5 hours, compared with 47.5 hours for Series 11. Charging also varied: our watch reached 58% and 72% after 30 minutes in separate tests, falling short of Apple’s claimed 80%. These results show that the Series 12 can comfortably exceed Apple’s 24-hour rating, but they don’t demonstrate a consistent improvement over Series 11. Actual battery life depends on usage.
A separate investigation by Macwelt’s Halyna Kubiv compared Series 11 and Series 12 during a seven-hour hike and subsequent everyday use. After the workout, Series 12 recorded more background activity but consumed less energy during the measured period. However, this was a one-day comparison with different conditions: Series 11 was actively paired with an iPhone and handling notifications, while Series 12 was not, and display use differed. 
Apple Watch Ultra 4
Battery life is one of Ultra 4’s biggest upgrades.
Apple rates it for:
50 hours normal use, up from 42 hours
84 hours Low Power Mode, up from 72 hours
18 hours standard outdoor workout tracking
25 hours Extended Workout
45 hours Max Extended Workout
Apple says the Extended Workout figure represents a 25 percent increase over the previous generation.
Apple says Ultra 4 can reach 80 percent in around 45 minutes, but 15 minutes of charging now provides up to 18 hours of use, versus 12 hours on Ultra 3.
Apple also credits more efficient workout algorithms with helping deliver the longer endurance.
Apple Watch charging
Both models use Apple’s magnetic fast-charging system with the Apple Watch Magnetic Fast Charger to USB-C Cable.
There is no change to the basic magnetic charging system this year.


						

							


Siri AI: Availability and requirements
Siri AI remains in beta, with availability depending on your language and region. The watchOS 27.2 update, released on October 26, adds French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish alongside English. Apple says Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish and Vietnamese will follow by the end of 2026.
Siri AI requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled device set to a supported language. It is currently unavailable on Apple Watch in the European Union and is not available to users under 13.


						

							


What is Audio Intelligence? 
Audio Intelligence is Apple’s collection of sound-based AI features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. It uses the watch’s microphones to recognize important sounds, identify music and, with forthcoming features, help you catch something you missed in a conversation or revisit its key points later.
Sound Recognition and automatic Music Recognition with Shazam are available now. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are due in beta later in 2026, initially in English, and require a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone. Here’s what each feature does and when you can use it.


						

							






Sound RecognitionAlerts you to sounds such as alarms and doorbellsAvailable now
Automatic Music RecognitionIdentifies background music in the Smart StackAvailable now
Live RewindDisplays the previous 15 seconds of speech as textBeta promised later in 2026
Siri RecapGenerates summaries of conversationsBeta promised later in 2026

 



Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 price
Apple has kept its entry prices unchanged in both the U.S. and U.K. – contrary to pre-event speculation that the Series 12 could increase in price.


Model2026 pricePrevious generation

Series 12 – U.S.42mm $399 / 46mm $449Series 11: 42mm $399 / 46mm $429
Series 12 – U.K.42mm £369 / 46mm £419Series 11: 42mm £369 / 46mm £399
Ultra 4 – U.S.From $799Ultra 3: $799
Ultra 4 – U.K.From £749Ultra 3: £749

 



Series 12 pricing varies considerably depending on case material. Aluminium is the entry-level option, while titanium costs more and the newly revived ceramic models occupy the premium end of the range.
Starting prices are unchanged, but the larger Series 12 costs more. The 46mm aluminum model starts at $449/£419 with GPS or $549/£519 with cellular—an increase of $20/£20 over the equivalent Series 11 models.
Should you buy Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people. It offers essentially all of Apple’s important new features – including the new Health Sensing System, Readiness, frequent HRV measurements, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence – in a considerably smaller and cheaper watch. (Live Rewind and Siri Recap are not available yet.)
However, our Series 12 review found inconsistent battery life and charging, along with occasional sluggishness. These observations may not reflect an established problem affecting every watch, but they temper our recommendation, particularly for owners of recent models considering an upgrade.
The strongest reason to choose Ultra 4 is battery life. Its increase in Apple’s rated battery life from 42 to 50 hours makes it much more practical for people who regularly spend more than a day away from a charger, while the new 25- and 45-hour extended workout modes make it substantially more appealing to runners, hikers, cyclists and endurance athletes.
Ultra 4 is also the better choice for outdoor adventurers because of its brighter 3,000-nit display, dual-frequency GPS, rugged titanium construction, Action button, 100m water resistance, recreational diving support and satellite communications. Series 12 is the better everyday watch: lighter, less bulky, available in two sizes and substantially cheaper.

title: Apple’s new iPad mini is a Duo you can’t close
content:
Macworld





There was no event, no livestream, no video presentation; just a press release and an update to Apple’s website. But as low-key, start-of-the-week product refreshes go, the 8th-gen iPad mini announcement was oddly impressive.
It has a much faster processor, jumping three generations from A17 Pro to A20 Pro. (Great news for those AI applications we all love so much.) It has a much better screen, going from LED to OLED with its deeper blacks and overall better color reproduction, while also becoming slightly larger (8.5 inches vs 8.3 inches) and considerably brighter (1,200 nits for HDR content vs 500 nits max). And the iPad itself has shrunk significantly in both thickness (6.3mm to 5.4mm) and weight (263 grams vs 297 grams), making it by far the most portable iPad yet.
Part of me applauds a valiant attempt to keep the iPad mini relevant instead of killing it off, as has seemed plausible at various stages in the product’s history. But another part thinks Apple has just responded to competition from the automobile industry by building the world’s fanciest horse and cart.
As I discussed briefly in our live blog for this week’s Apple announcements, the iPad mini’s great problem is that the ground has moved beneath its feet. When the device came out, an argument could be made that it was the best way for Apple fans to view movies and play games on the go. It was relatively cheap, portable, powerful, and above all delivered an experience you couldn’t get with any other Apple product. But that hasn’t been the case for some time now.

				
					

				
			
The iPad mini has a lot of the features of an iPhone Duo when opened.
Apple
Take the phablet, as we used to call very large smartphones before products of that form factor became normal and even expected. They threaten mini tablets because they approach the same problem in a more versatile way. Yes, an iPad mini is cheaper than an iPhone 18 Pro Max. But the latter is also a phone. It’s more portable, more powerful, offers a very respectable 6.9-inch screen that’s great for games and movies, and it’s the only mobile device you need. Why buy an iPad mini and a phone when you can get both in one package?
But this year the iPad mini’s situation became even more desperate with the launch of the iPhone Duo. The Duo has its issues, but beating any iPad mini in a head-to-head is not one of them. It’s just straight up better: infinitely more portable in its folded form, very nearly as large-screened when unfolded, and vastly more powerful and versatile. A world containing the iPhone Duo is not one that’s friendly to the iPad mini, which is essentially a Duo you can’t close.
Does the A20 Pro update change the equation in any meaningful way? Thinness is always nice, the mini needed an up-to-date processor for future-proofing if nothing else, and the OLED screen is the sort of quality-of-life upgrade you can market around. But it’s still fundamentally a product whose niche got swallowed up by something more exciting. It still feels kind of obsolete. It’s still a knife at a gunfight.
Can the iPad mini succeed? I think so. But my advice, perhaps counterintuitively, would be for Apple to embrace the qualities and characteristics that make it different from the bigger iPhones and the more powerful iPads. It needs to be cheaper, not thinner. It needs to be tougher, not more powerful. (The new model’s water and dust resistance is a bigger deal, in my opinion.) It needs to become the iPad equivalent of the old iPhone SE, by delivering an old-fashioned experience for the niche audience that doesn’t want the newer and more expensive version.
The iPad mini can find a role if it focuses on going to the places where you wouldn’t take an iPhone Duo, and doing the jobs that aren’t suitable for an iPad Air. I want it to be an extremely convenient ebook reader and web surfer that’s equally at home by the pool or on the coffee table, not yet another identikit reworking of the iPhone-iPad continuum that doesn’t make as much sense as the alternatives on either side.
The iPad mini isn’t going to beat the iPhone Duo by being better: the horse isn’t going to run faster than a car, and the cart isn’t going to offer more comfortable seats. It’s not going to do the same jobs to the same standard. But the mini is different, and it can still succeed if Apple embraces that.

title: Apple Creator Studio gets a major AI boost with latest update
content:
Macworld





On Tuesday, Apple announced new features in the apps for Apple Creator Studio, its collection of professional creative apps for Mac, iPhone, and iPad. The updates will be available in November for free to current Creator Studio subscribers. Each of the 10 apps that make up Creator Studio received a major update.
Video software updates
Apple acquired plug-in developer MotionVFX earlier this year; the company specialized in video editing and graphics tools subscriptions that cost for $29 per month. The MotionVFX tools for color grading, rotoscoping, and tracking, as well as graphics, themed templates, titles, and transitions will be incorporated into Final Cut Pro in the update for no extra charge.
Final Cut Pro now has cross-app functionality with Pixelmator Pro, so editors can open images directly from the timeline and save changes back to the project without needing to reimport the image. Other enhancements include more keyframe easing options, the ability to disconnect clips from the primary storyline to place them anywhere on the timeline, and 23 new transcription languages.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Motion also benefits from the MotionVFX acquisition; it incorporates new options for 3D camera tracking, cinematic color grading, and one-click selection for visual effects. Motion also supports a new Displacement filter, image generation and edits from text descriptions, cross-app functionality with Pixelmator Pro, and fine-tuned keyframe easing. Compressor supports the ability to encode Cinematic mode video recorded on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.
Pixelmator Pro
Pixelmator Pro gets the power of AI with its new Generate Fill option that performs edits based on a user’s description. It takes into account the surrounding area to match lighting, perspective, and texture to create a seamless blend. Sharpness is maintained with Pixelmator Pro’s built-in Super Resolution technology.
Logic Pro
Apple worked with OpenAI for a new intelligent assistant in Logic Pro for Mac. The assistant can be used for navigating workflow productions, refining an active project, starting a new song, or setting up a vocal track. The Browser has been redesigned to make it easier to find effect patches, instruments, loops, and more. Logic Pro can analyze and classify sounds to make them easier to find.
The enhanced Stem Splitter now has the ability to isolate, replace, or rebalance drum parts without needing the original multitracks. A new Sergio George Producer Pack features authentic Latin jazz and salsa loops, including a full salsa percussion section, brass ensemble, and basses.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Logic Pro also has a Voice Memo Studio Sound feature that can reduce noise in iPhone recordings. And Logic Pro on both the Mac and iPad has Liquid Glass Ui enhancements.
Freeform, Keynote, Numbers, Pages
Apple’s productivity apps are enhanced by a new “Intelligent Assistant” that understands document context and can be used to develop content. For example, the assistant in Keynote can be used to design slides. In Pages, the assistant can help with fine-tuning what’s been written. In Numbers, the assistant can calculate, visualize, and organize data, recommend chart types, and build custom tables. Apple accidentally revealed these features last week when it prematurely posted the update.
The Content Hub for these apps now includes Apple-curated stock video footage, and subscribers get new templates and themes. Keynote introduces support for Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), an open JSON-based bundle file format. Freeform adds text styles, and in December, will have the ability to edit images directly in Pixelmator Pro and generate editable shapes from text descriptions.
Apple Creator Studio is available via subscription for $12.99/£12.99 per month or $129/£129 per year. Education pricing is available. Up to six family members can share all of the apps and content included in Apple Creator Studio with Family Sharing. One-time-purchase versions of Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, Compressor, and MainStage are available on the Mac App Store. Freeform, Keynote, Numbers, and Pages are free.
